messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajiv had always found solace in the great outdoors. As a park ranger, he spent most days hiking through dense forests and maintaining the natural beauty of the land. But it was his role as a father that brought him the greatest joy. His young daughter, Leela, was the light of his life. So when she fell gravely ill with a rare disease at the age of seven, Rajiv's world came crashing down. The memories of those hospital days still lingered in his mind like a toxic cloud. He recalled the antiseptic smell that wafted through the corridors, the beeping of machines, and the endless stream of doctors and nurses rushing to save Leela's life. The fear of losing her was all-consuming, and Rajiv found himself constantly on edge, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Even now, years later, the slightest whiff of hospital smell could transport him back to those agonizing days. But it wasn't just the memories that haunted him – it was also the perceived injustices surrounding Leela's illness. He couldn't help but ruminate about how the doctors might have misdiagnosed her initially or how the insurance company had delayed coverage for a crucial treatment. His mind became fixated on ways to get even with those he felt were responsible, as if exacting revenge could somehow undo the past. As Rajiv delved deeper into his ruminations, he began to notice that certain smells triggered these vengeful thoughts. The smell of alcohol, which reminded him of a particularly contentious conversation with a doctor who had prescribed Leela's medication, would send him spiraling down a rabbit hole of anger and resentment. Even the feeling of dizziness or lightheadedness, which he often experienced when he stood up too quickly, could trigger these ruminations. Rajiv tried to avoid being reminded of those days by others. He would change the subject or excuse himself from conversations that touched on Leela's illness. But it was hard to escape the memories entirely, especially at work. The park's first aid station had a faint hospital smell that always caught him off guard. On more than one occasion, he found himself standing frozen in front of the station, his mind racing with thoughts of what could have been done differently. As time passed, Rajiv noticed that his fixation on revenge was starting to consume him. He began to withdraw from social interactions, preferring the solitude of the forest to the company of friends and family. His relationship with Leela's mother started to fray as well, as she grew tired of his constant brooding. It was then that Rajiv realized he needed help – not just for himself, but for those around him who were suffering because of his inability to let go. With a mix of trepidation and hope, Rajiv finally sought out therapy. He knew it wouldn't be easy to confront the demons that had haunted him for so long, but he was willing to try anything to break free from the cycle of rumination and pain. As he sat in the therapist's office, the familiar smell of wood polish transporting him back to his childhood home, Rajiv felt a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, he could learn to forgive and move forward.
